description: We are Team LunarSync. We are a group of Computer Science and Engineering students united by a shared passion for space exploration, scientific computing, and interactive data visualisation. Bringing together strengths in Python physics modelling, computer vision, geospatial data analysis, and full-stack web development, our team built the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser to make NASA’s complex lunar datasets instantly actionable.
summary:
Landing at the Moon’s South Pole is tough—steep slopes can tip a lander over, and a single mountain ridge can block sunlight or cut off radio contact with Earth for weeks. Normally, mission planners have to spend weeks cross-checking massive NASA terrain maps and orbital tables just to evaluate one landing spot.

We built the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser to do that work in seconds. Our web app combines NASA LOLA elevation models (5m–20m) and JPL Horizons data to reconstruct the exact 360-degree mountain skyline around South Pole targets like Shackleton Ridge, Mons Mouton, and Malapert A. Users can set a 10-day mission window and watch the Sun and Earth move across the peaks in real time, checking three essentials: safe slope (Land), solar wattage (Power), and Earth visibility (Data Transfer). We also added 500-point Monte Carlo landing simulations and OpenCV shadow checks against real LROC crater photos so teams can trust the numbers and plan safer touchdowns for future CLPS and Artemis missions.
details:
What it does

LunarSync's CLPS Lunar Mission Browser helps you choose where and when to land a small robotic lander near the Moon's south pole. You start by entering a basic mission plan:

• how many days the mission lasts

• when you want to land

• how much power the lander needs

• how many hours its batteries can survive in the dark

• how much contact with Earth you need

You then pick one of three real candidate sites: the Shackleton Connecting Ridge, Mons Mouton (near where Intuitive Machines' IM-2 landed), and Malapert A (where IM-1 Odysseus landed). The app shows, hour by hour across 2027, when the site gets sunlight, when it can see Earth, how steep the ground is, and whether your lander would get through the mission.

The south pole is a strange place. The Sun never rises more than a degree or two above the horizon, so a single nearby hill can throw a shadow for days. Earth also slips in and out of view. A spot that looks good on a map can still leave a lander frozen and out of contact. We wanted to make that visible in a way anyone can understand.

How it works

Everything is calculated ahead of time by a Python pipeline using real NASA data, then shown in a fast web app.

• Terrain: We use elevation maps from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). We use the sharpest map available for each site: 5 m per pixel at the ridge, 10 m at Mons Mouton and 20 m at Malapert A. A wider 60 m map covers the terrain farther away.

• Horizon: From each site we look out in 720 directions, every half degree, up to 255 km away. We record how high the skyline is in each direction and include the Moon's curvature.

• Sun and Earth positions: NASA's SPICE toolkit gives the exact positions of the Sun and Earth for every hour of 2027. We checked them against NASA JPL's Horizons system, and they matched to within a millionth of a degree.

• Partial sunlight: Near the pole, the Sun often sits half-hidden behind a ridge, so we don't treat sunlight as simply on or off. We calculate how much of the Sun's disk is actually visible, from 0% to 100%.

• Landing uncertainty: Landers never touch down exactly on target, so we scatter 500 possible landing points within 100 m of each site. Each point gets its own slope check (10° or less is safe) and its own horizon. We also add the known error in the LOLA height data, which shows how much the results could realistically shift.

• Mission windows: Every polar site has long nights at some point in the year. Instead of declaring a site "unsafe" forever, we ask whether your specific mission dates avoid the worst of it. The app suggests the best 10-day landing windows for each site. At Mons Mouton, for example, all 500 landing points pass in the best window. At Malapert A, at most 14.6% pass because the ground there slopes about 12°, the same tilt Odysseus landed on.

• Checking ourselves against real photos: We took a real photo from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera and used OpenCV to detect the shadows in it automatically. We then compared those shadows with what our model predicted for that exact moment. Every shadow we predicted was also in the photo, and we caught about 81% of the real shadows. We report these numbers as they came out and never tuned the model to look better.

Benefits and impact

Most of this kind of analysis lives in research papers and specialist tools. Our app puts it into an interactive planner that students, mission teams and curious members of the public can explore. It answers practical questions:

• If we land on this date, will the batteries make it through the night?

• Will we be able to talk to Earth?

• Is the ground flat enough?

NASA's CLPS program relies on commercial landers, and Artemis astronauts will head to this same region. Tools like this can help people understand why landing site and timing matter so much.

Tools and technologies

• Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, Numba for fast parallel horizon calculations, rasterio for reading the elevation maps, SpiceyPy for NASA SPICE, astroquery for JPL Horizons, OpenCV for the shadow check, and pydantic plus pytest for validation and testing.

• Web app: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, D3 for charts and maps, Zustand for state, and Zod to check that the data the app loads matches the expected format.

• Hosting: Vercel.

• NASA data: LOLA elevation models (NASA Goddard PGDA), NAIF SPICE kernels, JPL Horizons and LRO camera images.

What makes it creative

• Seeing the uncertainty: Instead of one number per site, you see a cloud of 500 possible landing points that change colour as you change the landing date. That shows how risky the choice really is.

• Planning around time: The app treats timing as part of site selection. The same spot can be excellent in one window and deadly in another.

• Showing our accuracy openly: A dedicated Data Accuracy page lists how many map pixels come from real laser measurements and how many are filled in between them. It also shows how our shadow predictions compare with real photos.

Factors we considered

• Honesty: We never tuned results toward a score we wanted. When a number looked physically odd, we stopped and investigated it. For example, the ridge site changes a lot with sensor height: about 58% sunlit at 2 m above the ground, about 91% at 5 m. We show that caveat in the app instead of hiding it.

• Real coordinates: All site locations come from published NASA and LROC sources.

• Realistic assumptions: Things like the 72-hour darkness limit and the 10-day mission length are realistic planning assumptions, and we label them that way, not as measurements.

• Speed and reliability: Everything is pre-calculated, so the app loads instantly and works without a live server.
